newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr claws back from earlier lows in late Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dlr claws back from earlier lows in late Tokyo.

text.p: 0600 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0600 GMT

The dollar clawed back from earlier lows against the yen in late Tokyo on Wednesday due to short-covering, prompted by worries over verbal intervention by Japanese monetary authorities and solid bids by investors.
Trade worries hovered in the background with Japan's current account surplus jumping in May, but that was mostly in line with expectations and failed to spur speculative dollar sales.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Finance Ministry said that the current account surplus, often a source of bitter rows with the United States, jumped in May to 906.8 billion yen from a 355.7 billion yen surplus a year earlier.
The dollar initially gained on the data but encountered a slew of sales from overseas operators and Japanese exporters above 113 yen, which knocked the dollar as low as 112.39 yen.

Ford Motor Co vice-chairman Wayne Booker, who was attending a meeting of the Japan-U.S. Business Council in San Francisco, said on Tuesday that a more appropriate dollar/yen exchange rate would be in the range of 100 to 110 yen.
The comments and lingering worries about Japan's surging surplus kept the dollar's recovery weak, dealers said.
Meanwhile, the weak Tokyo stock market and concerns about the talk-up of the dollar by Japanese officials limited the dollar's falls, they added.

"People went on alert when the dollar came close to 112 yen and were quick to cover their short positions," said a bank dealer. "The authorities were expected to start talking up the dollar at around 112 yen in a bid to deter it from falling to 110 yen," he added. Talk of bids by Japanese investors, including trust banks and public funds, supported the dollar.
There was vague speculation that a U.S.-based major hedge fund was buying dollars on dips in connection with Japanese authorities' efforts to stabilise the market.
Some traders said they were waiting for further news from the Japan-U.S. Business Council in San Francisco later in the day, but were becoming mixed about the dollar/yen's direction.
"Dollar/yen should be in a 111.00-113.50 yen trading band now. There's no real sentiment for it. It's just trading on official comments," said a European bank dealer in Singapore.
Traders seemed more confident in the mark's weakness, willing to sell marks for dollars and yen.
The dollar surpassed 1.76 marks overnight for the first time since February 1994, aided by broad mark weakness after weak German job report and expectations of higher U.K. interest rates.

Dealers in Tokyo said offers by European operators at just above 1.7600 marks checked its advance but U.S. operators were bullish on the dollar's rise against the mark. Some were expecting it to climb to 1.78 marks in the medium term.
"There is like a consensus that the European single currency will start with a weak value. This general sense could keep the mark weak for a while," said a Japanese bank dealer.
The mark fell as low as near a two-year low of 63.85 yen in morning Tokyo. Japanese exporters and overseas operators were keen to sell marks for yen, Tokyo dealers said.
It was at around 64.18/21 yen at 0707 GMT.
A Singapore dealer said mark/yen looked fairly well bid but a breach of the 63.80 level on the downside would expose it to a slew of stop-loss sales.
"I'm hearing there's a yard of stop-loss sales below 63.80. If it breaks, it could easily go to 63.50/60," he said.
